options: Any instrument traded on the New York Stock Exchange
A group of instruments that share risk/return characteristics and tend to be regulated similarly
Any investment that pays a fixed rate of interest
A single company's stock and bonds combined
questions.explain: An asset class groups instruments that behave similarly in the market and face similar regulatory treatment, such as equities or fixed income.

questions.q: Which asset class is best described as "ownership shares in a company"?
options: Fixed income
Commodities
Equities
Cash and money market instruments
questions.explain: Equities (stocks) represent ownership shares, giving the holder a claim on future profits and usually a vote in corporate decisions.

questions.q: On the risk-return spectrum described in this lesson, where do Treasury bills and cash sit relative to equities?
options: At roughly the same risk level as equities
At the high-risk end, above equities
At the low-risk end, below equities
Risk-return spectrums don't apply to cash instruments
questions.explain: Cash and Treasury bills sit at the low end of the spectrum — close to risk-free — while equities carry higher expected risk and return.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat derivatives as different in kind from the other six asset classes?
options: Derivatives are always riskier than any other asset class
Derivatives are only used by hedge funds, not other investors
A derivative's value is derived from an underlying asset rather than being a direct claim itself
Derivatives cannot be traded on an exchange
questions.explain: Equities, bonds, commodities, currencies, cash, and alternatives are direct claims on something real. A derivative instead derives its value from an underlying asset and has no independent existence.

questions.q: A trader buys a call option purely to speculate, while a portfolio manager buys the same type of option to protect an existing stock position. What does this illustrate about derivatives risk?
options: Options are always safe regardless of how they're used
A derivative's risk depends on how it's used, not on the instrument type alone
Only portfolio managers are allowed to use derivatives for hedging
Speculative use and hedging use always carry identical risk
questions.explain: The same derivative contract can increase risk when used to speculate or reduce risk when used to hedge — risk depends on the position it's added to, not the instrument alone.
